summary: The letter's most famous arc: you were dead — walking according to the course of this world, children of wrath like everyone else — and God, rich in mercy, made you alive with Christ, raised you with him, and seated you with him in the heavenly places. Saved by grace through faith, not of works; created for the good works God prepared. Then the chapter turns to the wall: Gentiles once far off, without hope and without God, are made near in Christ's blood — the middle wall broken, the two made one new humanity, both reconciled in one body through the cross, and the whole company growing into a temple God lives in.
whyItMatters: This chapter carries the letter's two great contributions in one breath — salvation by grace (2:8-9) and the two-become-one reconciliation (2:14-18) — and refuses to let them be separated: the same grace that raises the dead also tears down the wall between peoples. Nearly every later reading of the letter's practical chapters stands on what this chapter settles.

context.author: Paul, speaking in the chapter's own words as one who was there: 'we also all once lived among them' (2:3) — the 'we' of Jews and the 'you' of Gentiles (2:11) both told from inside the story.
context.audience: Gentile believers, addressed directly: 'you, the Gentiles in the flesh, who are called "uncircumcision"' (2:11) — and told to 'remember' what they once were (2:11-12).
context.date: Undated; the chapter's timeline is the reader's — 'once' dead, 'now' made near (2:13), with 'the ages to come' still ahead to display the riches of grace (2:7).
context.setting: A mixed congregation of former 'circumcision' and 'uncircumcision' — the chapter's middle section exists because the two groups now share one table, one body, one Spirit.
context.literaryForm: Two movements: the dead-raised arc (2:1-10) told at preaching pace, then the far-off-brought-near arc (2:11-22) that shifts from 'you' to 'we both' as the wall comes down.

outline.heading: Dead, and made alive
outline.note: The former walk according to the course of this world, under the prince of the power of the air; 'we also' once lived in the lusts of the flesh, children of wrath — but God, rich in mercy, made us alive together with Christ: 'by grace you have been saved.'

outline.heading: Raised, seated, and saved by grace
outline.note: Raised and seated with him in the heavenly places; the ages to come will show the exceeding riches of his grace; saved through faith, not of yourselves, not of works — created in Christ Jesus for the good works God prepared beforehand.

outline.heading: Remember what you were
outline.note: Once Gentiles in the flesh, called uncircumcision by the circumcision; separate from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world.

outline.heading: Made near, and the wall broken
outline.note: In Christ's blood the far off are made near; he is our peace, making both one, breaking down the middle wall, abolishing the hostility in his flesh to create one new humanity — reconciling both in one body through the cross, and preaching peace to the far and the near, access in one Spirit to the Father.

outline.heading: Fellow citizens, a building, a dwelling
outline.note: No longer strangers but fellow citizens with the saints and of God's household; built on the foundation of apostles and prophets, Christ the cornerstone; the whole building growing into a holy temple — a habitation of God in the Spirit.

keyVerses.text: for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast.
keyVerses.why: The letter's most-quoted claim about how anyone stands before God — a completed rescue ('have been saved'), by grace, through faith, with boasting excluded.

keyVerses.text: For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation, having abolished in his flesh the hostility, the law of commandments contained in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man of the two, making peace,
keyVerses.why: The chapter's second great claim: the same work of Christ that saves individuals also reconciles peoples — the wall between Jew and Gentile is not lowered but broken.

keyVerses.text: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.
keyVerses.why: The verse that keeps grace from being passivity: rescued apart from works, then created for works already prepared — the 'walk' that organizes chapters 4–6 begins here.

themes: from death to life with Christ

questions.question: In what sense were the readers 'dead' in trespasses and sins?
questions.answer: The chapter describes a life, not a metaphor only: they walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, among the lusts of the flesh, 'children of wrath, even as the rest' (2:1-3). Death here is separation from God's life — a real condition the chapter says God cured by a real act: 'made us alive together with Christ' (2:5).

questions.question: Who is 'the prince of the power of the air'?
questions.answer: The phrase names a ruler over the 'air' — the realm between earth and heaven in the ancient picture of the world. The chapter gives him a present tense activity: 'the spirit who now works in the children of disobedience' (2:2). The letter does not name him here, but its later armor passage points the same direction — 'the wiles of the devil' (6:11).

questions.question: Does 'not of works, that no one would boast' contradict being 'created for good works'?
questions.answer: The chapter puts the two three verses apart on purpose: salvation is 'not of works' (2:9) — no one earns it — and yet we are 'created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them' (2:10). The order is the answer: works are never the cause of salvation, always its prepared result. The verse is the hinge between the letter's first half and its walk-instructions.

questions.question: What is 'the middle wall of separation' that was broken?
questions.answer: The picture is physical — a dividing wall — and most readers hear the temple's real barrier, the wall that kept Gentiles out of the inner courts on pain of death. Paul says Christ 'broke down the middle wall' and 'abolished in his flesh the hostility, the law of commandments contained in ordinances' (2:14-15). What exactly the abolishing means for the law is argued across traditions; the chapter's own claim is stated plainly: the purpose was 'one new man of the two, making peace.'

questions.question: Why does Paul tell them to 'remember' what they were?
questions.answer: 'Therefore remember' (2:11) — the chapter makes memory a discipline: once separate from Christ, alienated from Israel's commonwealth, strangers to the covenants of promise, 'having no hope and without God in the world' (2:12). Remembering is not shame; it is the only way the words 'but now' (2:13) land with their full weight.

questions.question: What does it mean that he 'came and preached peace to you who were far off and to those who were near'?
questions.answer: The line echoes Isaiah's promise of peace to him 'who is far off and him who is near' (Isaiah 57:19), and the chapter applies it to Christ himself: preaching through the apostles and witnesses, both groups — Gentiles 'far off' and Jews 'near' — heard the same message (2:17). The result is one access: 'through him we both have our access in one Spirit to the Father' (2:18).

questions.question: Why the shift from a building to a growing temple to a habitation?
questions.answer: The images stack on purpose: the readers are 'fellow citizens' (a civic image), 'God's household' (a family image), and a building 'being fitted together' on the foundation of apostles and prophets with Christ as cornerstone — and then the building does what buildings do not: it 'grows into a holy temple in the Lord' (2:19-21). The mixing of living and built images says the people are the place: 'a habitation of God in the Spirit' (2:22).

questions.question: Why 'seated us with him in the heavenly places' — is that future or now?
questions.answer: The chapter's verbs are past: God 'raised us up with him, and made us to sit with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus' (2:6). Whatever the letter means by seating, it presents it as already done in Christ — the same language it used for Christ himself in 1:20. The purpose clause that follows explains why it is stated now: so that 'in the ages to come' God can show the exceeding riches of his grace (2:7).

questions.question: What does 'workmanship' mean in verse 10?
questions.answer: The Greek word is poiēma — a made thing, a work. The hosted text keeps 'workmanship': 'we are his workmanship' — the ones who could not save ourselves are God's own handiwork, made for a purpose he prepared in advance. The word quietly finishes the chapter's argument: the saved are not self-made, and their works are not self-assigned.

glossary.def: A made thing — poiēma in Greek; the believers are God's handiwork, created for prepared good works (2:10).
The chapter's image for what divided Jew and Gentile — heard by most readers against the temple's real barrier courts; Christ is said to have broken it down (2:14).
The civic half of the new status: Gentile believers are no longer strangers but citizens with the saints and members of God's household (2:19).
